newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.N. team hunts for missing Rwanda refugees.
newsitem.headline: U.N. team hunts for missing Rwanda refugees.

text.p: The U.N. said on Thursday it sent an assessment team into eastern Zaire's Bukavu to track down up to 700,000 missing Rwandan Hutu refugees central to debate over planned military intervention.

"A U.N. assessment team is in Bukavu evaluating possibilities. It is absolutely essential to have staff in the region," Peter Kessler, U.N. refugee agency (UNHCR) spokesman in Nairobi said. "We are absolutely desperate to locate these 700,000."
Zairean rebels have until now prevented aid agencies from entering Bukavu to gain first hand picture.
Kessler told Reuters the rebels, backed by Rwanda, had told the team all the camps in the area were empty and the refugees had fled several hundred km (miles) westwards and southwards.
"But I stress, there is no independent confirmation of that, that is why we need people in there," he said.

The United Nation's World Food Programme (WFP) reported on Wednesday "strong indications" that more than 100,000 refugees could be heading for Goma from Bukavu, but said early on Thursday they may have stopped moving.
"We got another report last night basically corroborating the existence of a large group, but this report indicates they may have stopped moving," WFP spokesperson Michele Quintaglie said.
The four-member assessment team comprising UNHCR, WFP, the U.N. Children's Fund and a British army official was expected to return to Cyangugu on Rwanda's Zaire border later on Thursday.

Canada said most nations involved in the humanitarian crisis in eastern Zaire believed a military force was still needed to deliver aid to more than a million Hutu refugees and displaced Zaireans wandering the bush after fleeing fighting between the Zaire army and ethnic Tutsi rebels.
But Ottawa's Deputy Foreign Minister Gordon Smith said military planners needed to develop a range of options -- including not sending ground troops at all.
Smith spoke at a news conference after a series of meetings at the United Nations, one of which involved representatives from 60 countries, including states who volunteered troops.
"Virtually all countries, including Zaire...believe that a military force is still required," he said.

"The conclusions of the meetings today are that the military planners need to develop options," Smith said. "The options of course include a zero option -- that there is no need for a military force to provide security to humanitarian relief organisations."

About 500,000 Hutu refugees have now returned to Rwanda to escape war pitting Zairean rebels supported by Rwanda against soldiers from Rwanda's Hutu-dominated former army and Hutu militias who led the 1994 genocide of Rwanda's minority Tutsis.

In an interview broadcast on Thursday, Zaire's ailing ruler Mobutu Seke Seko told CNN he was "fine" and promised to return home from the Frence Riviera once his recovery from cancer treatment was complete.

He termed the rebels who have taken over a swath of eastern Zaire and their supporters as "devils" who profited from his absence, adding: "They stabbed me in the back while I was away. Do you think this would have happened if I were there? No. Never."
But he refused to be drawn into a discussion of whether the Zaire army would regroup and retake eastern Zaire.
"My watchword these days is peace. If things get worse in eastern Zaire after I return, I can assure you it won't be Zaire's fault," he said in reply.
Zaire on Wednesday suspended its army chief, General Eluki Monga for breaking ranks and arguing against U.N. intervention, in a potentially dangerous split in the country's hierarchy.
Eluki had told French radio that the intervention of a U.N. force was now unnecessary and repeated complaints by the army that the government was not giving it the means to battle rebels.
